title: prevention of occupationally acquired infections among heath-care workers
display_name: Prevention of Occupationally Acquired Infections Among Heath-care Workers
abstract: hospitals and medical clinics are favorable settings for the transmission of infectious diseases because infected and susceptible persons are brought into close proximity. health-care workers (hcw) are at particular risk because their work demands close contact with patients who may be harboring pathogenic microorganisms. this article focuses on the prevention of occupationally acquired infectious diseases among hcw, although it should be recognized that a comprehensive occupational health program also reduces the risk of hospital-acquired infection among patients. occupational infections among microbiology laboratory workers that are not common to other hcw will not be discussed.there are four critical infection prevention strategies: 1) ensuring immunity of hcw to vaccine-preventable diseases, 2) using isolation precautions to prevent transmission of microorganisms from patients to hcw, 3)evaluating and managing hcw exposed to communicable diseases, and 4)evaluating and managing hcw who have communicable diseases. applying these strategies effectively requires collaboration among the occupational health service, the infection control department, managers of hospital departments,and hcw.preplacement screening of hcw for immunity to vaccine-preventable diseases and vaccination of non-immune individuals can minimize the potential for these diseases among hcw and, hence, transmission to susceptible patients. the costs for preplacement screening and vaccination of hcw should be borne by the health-care organization for legal and ethical reasons and to enhance cooperation and compliance with the program. moreover, such a strategy usually is more cost-effective than trying to control an outbreak of a highly communicable disease, such as measles.occupational health departments should be thoroughly familiar with guidelines for vaccination of adults, including the precautions and contraindications for specific vaccinations.transmission of measles in health-care facilities was a serious problem during the upsurge of the disease that occurred in the united states in the late 1980s and early 1990s. although the majority of cases of nosocomial measles occurred in susceptible children, numerous cases occurred in hcw. furthermore, although persons born before 1957 traditionally were considered to be immune to measles, nearly one third of measles cases in hcw in the past decade occurred in persons born before 1957.a quality standard for ensuring measles immunity among hcw has been developed by the infectious diseases society of america and published widely in an effort to reduce the incidence of occupationally acquired measles in this population. acceptable criteria of immunity to measles are listed in table 1. notably, an undocumented history of measles or birth prior to 1957 is not considered sufficient proof of immunity. recommendations for vaccination of persons who have no evidence of immunity also are listed in table 1. the cost-effectiveness of various strategies for dealing with hcw who have no proof of vaccination or physician-diagnosed measles has not been studied in depth. for instance, it remains to be determined whether it is preferable to vaccinate these individuals or to obtain serologic tests from all of them, then vaccinate only nonimmune persons.nosocomial mumps and rubella are much less common among hcw, but the consequences of these infections can be significant. mumps can result in orchitis and possibly sterility among men, and congenital rubella syndrome may develop in the fetus of a pregnant woman. immunity should be assessed and vaccination provided for nonimmune hcw as described in table 1. recent studies have shown no risk of long-term arthritis following immunization of susceptible women. as noted for measles, the cost-effectiveness of strategies for dealing with hcw who have no proof of vaccination or physician-diagnosed mumps or rubella has not been determined.in contrast to other vaccine-preventable diseases, a verbal history of varicella is sufficient proof of immunity among hcw, as are the other criteria listed in table 1. reliance on verbal history may change in ensuing decades if naturally occurring varicella declines as a result of the use of the varicella vaccine. eighty percent or more of hcw who have no verbal history of varicella have evidence of prior infection as determined by serologic testing. a commercially available latex agglutination test can be completed rapidly and is comparable to other serologic tests (eg, fluorescent antibody membrane antigen test, indirect fluorescent antibody test,glycoprotein enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) in assessing natural immunity.varicella vaccine should be used to vaccinate nonimmune hcw according to the schedule in table 1. after the second dose of vaccine, most healthy adults ( 99%) develop an antibody response. for this reason, and because reliable serologic tests for vaccine-induced production of antibody are not readily available (the previously noted latex agglutination test is not sufficiently reliable for this purpose), routine tests of postvaccination immunity are not recommended.about 10% of adult vaccine recipients develop a rash in the 3 weeks after immunization, which may occur at the inoculation site or in a general distribution. live vaccine virus has been recovered from skin lesions, and transmission to susceptible contacts has been documented, although the risk of this occurrence appears to be less than 1%. nonetheless, vaccinated hcw should examine themselves daily during the 3 weeks after vaccination and report any rash to the occupational health service. at our hospital, we take the precaution of restricting hcw who have a postvaccination rash from patient care until further information about the risk of transmission of vaccine virus in the health-care setting is known.the incidence of occupationally acquired hepatitis b has declined significantly in the past decade, probably due to wider use of hepatitis b vaccine, although other prevention measures (eg, universal precautions,needleless intravenous infusion systems) also may have played roles. nonetheless, many hcw still have not been vaccinated and are susceptible to infection.the occupational safety and health administration (osha) requires hospitals to assess the immunity to hepatitis b among hcw. criteria for immunity are listed in table 1. if there is no documented history of prior infection or receipt of hepatitis b vaccine, it is not necessary to perform serologic tests for hepatitis b surface antigen (hbsag) or antibody to hepatitis b surface antigen (anti-hbs) before initiating the vaccine series,although these tests may be used in settings in which prior infection is common enough for prevaccination screening to be cost-effective. osha requires that nonimmune hcw be offered hepatitis b vaccination free-of-charge and that hcws who do not wish to be vaccinated decline such immunization in writing. vaccine should be administered to unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated hcw as described in table 1.postvaccination screening for anti-hbs after the third vaccine dose should be performed to identify persons who have not developed a protective level of anti-hbs (>10 miu/ml) and are considered nonresponders. approximately 10% of hcw who receive the three-dose series are nonresponders. about 30% of these individuals will develop protective levels of anti-hbs after an additional vaccine dose, and an additional 60% will develop protective levels after three additional vaccine doses. revaccinated hcw should be retested for anti-hbs after completion of the revaccination series. if they do not respond to revaccination, no additional vaccination is warranted.although anti-hbs levels decline in the decade after vaccination, data suggest that protection against hepatitis b virus infection is maintained among hcw who responded to the vaccine. consequently, routine booster doses are not recommended.nosocomial transmission of influenza occurs in association with seasonal community outbreaks. hcw are at risk of acquiring the infection in their home or community or from hospitalized patients. annual vaccination is necessary because immunity to particular subtypes is relatively short-lived, and the antigenic composition of circulating subtypes changes from year to year. unfortunately, numerous studies have documented relatively poor( 30%) acceptance of annual influenza vaccine by hcw. one obstacle is the common misconception that vaccination is associated with significant adverse effects. another is the perception that the vaccine does not offer significant protection against infection. consequently, strategies must be undertaken to increase vaccine acceptance among hcw. we distribute educational pamphlets about the vaccine, advertise the vaccination campaign extensively,set up vaccination booths in the main hospital lobby, and bring the vaccine to the staff in their work areas. although we have not performed a formal analysis, we believe that the expense of the campaign is offset by fewer lost days of work due to influenza. recent studies have suggested that an intranasal vaccine is highly effective, which may make immunization more acceptable in the future.diphtheria in hospitalized children in the united states is extremely rare. however, this disease is not uncommon in other countries; consequently, hcw should be screened for completion of the primary immunization series and receipt of booster doses at appropriate intervals, especially in areas that have substantial immigrant populations. if more than 10 years have elapsed since completion of the primary series or since the individual received the last booster dose, the hcw should be given a booster dose of diphtheria-tetanus vaccine. most occupational health services do not provide diphtheria-tetanus vaccine to hcw, but they should remind hcw to obtain the necessary doses from their primary health-care providers.exposure to pertussis is a persistent problem for hcw caring for hospitalized children. in addition, adults often serve as a reservoir for the organism, with subsequent transmission to children. in contrast to the other diseases listed in table 1, it is difficult to assess immunity to pertussis. receipt of the primary vaccine series and two booster doses by the child does not guarantee immunity in adulthood, and serologic correlates of pertussis immunity are not well defined. unfortunately, booster doses of whole cell vaccine cannot be given to adults because of the high incidence of adverse effects. the recently developed acellular pertussis vaccine may boost immunity to pertussis in adults who have less reactogenicity, and there may be a role for this vaccine in protecting hcw from occupationally acquired pertussis in the future.a number of clusters of nosocomial tuberculosis were reported in united states hospitals in the 1990s. although most occurred in patients, some hcw also became infected. in some cases, infection with multi-drug-resistant mycobacterium tuberculosis resulted in the death of the hcw. in each instance, breakdowns in the proper identification, treatment, or isolation of patients who had active pulmonary tuberculosis were identified. because of these events, the role of bacillus calmette gue rin (bcg) vaccination for hcw has been reexamined, although it still is not recommended for routine use. bcg vaccination may be considered in unusual situations in which the likelihood of transmission of m tuberculosis strains resistant to isoniazid or rifampin is high and standard infection prevention measures have been fully implemented and determined to be unsuccessful in reducing the risk.effective use of isolation precautions can minimize the risk of transmission of microorganisms in hospitals. in 1996, the hospital infection control practices advisory committee to the centers for disease control and prevention (cdc) issued a revised guideline for isolation precautions in hospitals. the guideline contains two tiers of precautions: standard and transmission-based.standard precautions replace two previous precautions systems: universal precautions (up) and body substance isolation (bsi). up was developed in 1985 to protect hcw from exposure to bloodborne pathogens, including hepatitis b virus and human immunodeficiency virus (hiv). bsi, developed in 1987, advocated the use of barriers (eg, gloves) to prevent contact with moist body surfaces and mucous membranes as well as blood and body fluids. the intent of bsi was to protect hcw from bloodborne pathogens and to prevent cross-infection due to contamination of individuals hands while they cared for patients who had undetected colonization with nosocomial pathogens (eg,antimicrobial-resistant microorganisms). standard precautions synthesize these two goals into a new system that is easier to apply. such precautions should be used for all patients regardless of diagnosis or presumed infection status during planned or potential contact with blood, all body fluids, and moist body surfaces.transmission-based precautions are designed to be used in addition to standard precautions in the care of patients who are known or suspected of being infected with epidemiologically important pathogens that can be transmitted by airborne, droplet, or contact routes. airborne precautions are designed to prevent transmission of microorganisms (eg, m tuberculosis, measles virus, varicella zoster virus) that are spread via droplet nuclei (respiratory droplets 5 mcm in size) generated by sneezing or coughing and that travel only short distances (<3 ft) before settling. contact precautions are designed to prevent the spread of microorganisms transmitted by direct or indirect physical contact, such as enteropathogens, respiratory viruses, and bacteria present in abscesses and wound infections. some pathogens require combinations of these precautions. for example, varicella requires airborne and contact precautions because the virus can be spread both by droplet nuclei and by direct contact with vesicles. specific components of standard and transmission-based precautions are discussed in detail in a recent publication(see garner in suggested reading).it is important to note that handwashing is an integral part of both standard and transmission-based precautions. this single intervention remains vastly underused by most hcw. moreover, many do not recognize that the use of gloves does not obviate the need for handwashing. although gloves may reduce contamination of hands, they often have macroscopic and microscopic holes that may result in hand contamination. further, hands also may become contaminated during removal of soiled gloves. consequently, hcw must wash their hands immediately after removing gloves. handwashing with standard soap and water is sufficient in most settings; the detergent effect of the soap and friction from rubbing hands together combine to remove microorganisms. handwashing with soaps containing topical antimicrobial agents will reduce counts of resident and transient microbial flora further and should be considered when caring for high-risk patients (eg, intensive care unit patients, immunocompromised patients) and before performing invasive procedures. use of waterless handwashing agents (eg, alcohols combined with emollients) is an alternative if handwashing with soap and water is inconvenient or difficult.table 2contains specific criteria for determining whether hcw have been exposed to a communicable disease as well as work restrictions and management recommendations for exposed individuals. additional comments about these diseases as well as the management of hcw exposed to active tuberculosis or bloodborne viruses (tables 3 and 4)are discussed below.measles vaccine (or mmr) prevents infection after exposure to measles if administered within 72 hours of exposure, although protection against disease is not complete (see table 2). immune globulin may prevent or at least modify disease if administered within 6 days of exposure and should be given to exposed persons for whom vaccine is contraindicated or those who do not receive vaccine within 72 hours.neither mumps nor rubella vaccines (nor mmr) prevents infection after exposure, although vaccine still should be administered to provide protection against subsequent exposures. mumps immune globulin is not effective and is not manufactured or licensed in the united states. limited data suggest that administration of immune globulin during the first trimester may lower the risk of congenital rubella syndrome in nonimmune, exposed, pregnant women, but breakthrough infection is common, and immune globulin is not recommended routinely for this purpose.varicella zoster immune globulin (vzig) prevents or reduces the severity of infection in nonimmune persons. nonimmune pregnant or immunocompromised hcw exposed to varicella should be given vzig as soon as possible after the exposure and within 96 hours of the exposure because of the high risk of severe disease in these individuals (table 2). vzig may be considered for otherwise healthy adults, but such an approach prolongs the period that these people must be excluded from patient care. because acyclovir can be administered to hcw who develop varicella, use of vzig can be avoided in low-risk individuals or in situations in which the degree of exposure was minor or questionable (see evaluation and management). the decision to administer vzig to healthy adult hcw usually is at the discretion of the individual and his or her health-care practitioner.vaccinated hcw exposed to varicella do not need to be checked for immunity because the two-dose vaccination schedule results in seroconversion in 99% of vaccinated adults. nonetheless, breakthrough varicella still is possible, even among vaccinated persons, although disease among these persons usually is milder than among unvaccinated persons. consequently, vaccinated hcw should monitor themselves closely for symptoms and signs of incipient varicella and be excluded from patient care if infection develops. in situations where an exposed, vaccinated hcw provides care for nonimmune,high-risk patients (eg, immunocompromised patients and patients at risk for severe complications of varicella), antibody testing may be helpful. if the latex agglutination antibody test result is positive, the person is unlikely to develop breakthrough varicella. if the test result is negative, additional testing should be considered for two reasons. first, exposure may boost antibody levels sufficiently for a repeat test 5 to 6 days later to be positive. second, the latex agglutination test is not especially reliable for detecting antibody that develops after vaccination (see ensuring immunity), so use of a more sensitive assay may document the presence of antibody. if repeat testing does not demonstrate antibody, it must be assumed that the hcw may develop varicella. these individuals should not care for high-risk patients;some hospitals may choose to exclude them from all patient care. if allowed to continue working, these individuals should be monitored closely and excluded from patient care if infection develops. additional experience with the management of vaccinated hcw will help to clarify the appropriate management of these individuals when they are exposed to varicella.two other interventions may be considered, although their effectiveness as prophylactic measures have not been established and their use is not recommended. the varicella vaccine has shown promising results in several trials of postexposure prophylaxis. another small study found that oral acyclovir administered for 1 week beginning on the eighth day after exposure markedly reduced the incidence of clinical disease and did not prevent seroconversion.administration of the current influenza vaccine to unvaccinated hcw is appropriate after exposure to an infected patient or coworker or in the setting of an institutional outbreak of influenza because it may provide immunity to other circulating strains (table 2). however, because the development of an immune response can take up to 2 weeks, vaccination is not likely to prevent infection following obvious exposure. to prevent disease when the risk of infection with influenza a is high or the consequences of infection are potentially severe(eg, hcw providing care to high-risk patients), chemoprophylaxis may be administered for 2 weeks after vaccination (table 2). in addition, chemoprophylaxis may be used during periods of peak influenza activity for hcw who cannot be vaccinated or who are providing care to high-risk patients if an outbreak is caused by a variant of influenza a that may not be controlled by the current vaccine.hcw who are exposed to title: the aetiology of maculopapular rash diseases in niter i, state of rio de janeiro, brazil: implications for measles surveillance
display_name: The aetiology of maculopapular rash diseases in Niterói, State of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil: implications for measles surveillance
abstract: a study investigating the causes of rash diseases using systematic laboratory testing was conducted in niter i, rio de janeiro, between january 1994 to april 1998. sera from 327 patients were tested for evidence of anti-rubella virus, measles virus, human parvovirus b19 and dengue fever virus specific immunoglobulin igm and anti-human herpes virus type 6 (hhv-6) igg antibodies. a laboratory confirmed diagnosis was achieved in 71 3% of the cases investigated: dengue fever (33 0%), rubella (20 2%), parvovirus b19 (9 2%), measles (6 7%) and hhv-6 (2 1%). no diagnosis was established for 94 cases (28 7%). an outbreak of measles was detected during 1997, with a peak in september and october. all of the diseases studied here presented with clinical features similar to measles and classical symptoms were found in all measles confirmed cases. the large overlap of combinations of signs and symptoms seen in this study highlights the difficulties of diagnosing a rash illness on clinical grounds alone.

title: agranulocytosis in a patient with acute parvovirus b19 infection: a case study
display_name: Agranulocytosis in a patient with acute Parvovirus B19 infection: a case study
abstract: the definition of neutropenia is the reduction in the absolute number of neutrophils below 1.5 10 9 . the chapter about acquired neutropenias affecting the adult population is of particular interest to the internist. pc, 75 years old man, was hospitalized because of fever, asthenia. in anamnesis: recent diagnosis of ulcerative pancolitis treated with mesalazine and corticosteroid therapy. during the hospitalization, to the fever resolution, we witnessed to a gradual reduction in the value of neutrophils leucocytes until the complete agranulocytosis. we set a therapy with granulocytes colony stimulating factors, and antifungal. the osteo-medullar biopsy confirmed a pure aplasia of the granulocyte marrow series without any evidence of cancer. the subsequent clinical development was favorable, with stable apyrexia and recovery of leucocytes count. few days after, we received the positive response on the research of anti-parvovirus b19 immunoglobulin m and in qualitative polymerase chain reaction. the patient was discharged with diagnosis agranulocytosis in patient with acute infection of parvovirus b19 . neutropenia associated with parvovirus infection is not frequent and is related to the presence of hematological diseases or condition of immunosuppression. the peculiarity of the case described is the complete agranulocytosis found: in fact in literature, only rare cases are described. patient gave his informed consent.

title: the role of parvovirus b19 infection in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
display_name: THE ROLE OF PARVOVIRUS B19 INFECTION IN CHILDHOOD ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA
abstract: the authors hypothesized that parvovirus b19 with its hematotropic effects has the potential to precipitate varying forms of cytopenia in patients prior to or at the diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (all). consequently, and in view of the increasing number of cases reported, this retrospective study evaluated, for the first time, the possible role of parvovirus b19 infection in pediatric patients suffering from all, by investigating the frequency and clinical relevance of this infection at the time of the malignant diagnosis or, when applicable, during a phase of pre-all. furthermore, a review of reported parvovirus b19 infections in pediatric all patients is presented. the serum of 65 consecutive pediatric patients with a diagnosis of all was examined for possible parvovirus b19 infection employing the polymerase chain reaction and elisa techniques. specific igg was demonstrated in 30% of the patients. one patient diagnosed with pre-all had evidence of parvovirus b19 dna in the serum during pancytopenia 5 months prior to the onset of all. the results suggest that there is an insignificant chance of finding a parvovirus b19 infection in pediatric patients with all at the time of diagnosis. however, parvovirus b19 infection may infrequently serve as a prodrome to all.

title: takotsubo syndrome associated with covid-19
display_name: Takotsubo Syndrome Associated with COVID-19
abstract: objective: the availability of public health information for optimised supportive care is critical during the covid-19 pandemic. we describe the first case of covid-19 complicated by takotsubo cardiomyopathy. materials and methods: we report the clinical, laboratory and radiological findings of a patient with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (sars-cov-2). results: the nasopharyngeal swab was positive for sars-cov-2 and x-ray images demonstrated pathognomonic pneumonia. the patient developed tachycardia and the echocardiogram confirmed the diagnosis of takotsubo cardiomyopathy. conclusions: doctors should be aware of the need to thoroughly study this new infection in order to understand its underlying mechanisms and related complications.

title: hydroxychloroquine in a g6pd-deficient patient with covid-19 complicated by haemolytic anaemia: culprit or innocent bystander
display_name: Hydroxychloroquine in a G6PD-Deficient Patient with COVID-19 Complicated by Haemolytic Anaemia: Culprit or Innocent Bystander
abstract: hydroxychloroquine has been used worldwide as a first-line treatment for patients hospitalized with covid-19. little is known about covid-19 and its effects on patients with congenital red blood cell disorders. we report a case of haemolytic anaemia in a 32-year-old patient and a fortuitous highlighting of g6pd deficiency. we reviewed the literature to assess the risk of hydroxychloroquine use in this context.

abstract: background and objective: recent evidence has linked childhood antibiotic use and microbiome disturbance to autoimmune conditions. this study tested the hypothesis that antibiotic exposure was associated with newly diagnosed juvenile idiopathic arthritis (jia). methods: we performed a nested case control study in a population-representative medical records database from the united kingdom. children with newly diagnosed jia were compared with age- and gender-matched control subjects randomly selected from general practices containing at least 1 case, excluding those with inflammatory bowel disease, immunodeficiency, or other systemic rheumatic diseases. conditional logistic regression was used to examine the association between antibacterial antibiotics (including number of antibiotic courses and timing) and jia after adjusting for significant confounders. results: any antibiotic exposure was associated with an increased rate of developing jia (adjusted odds ratio: 2.1 [95% confidence interval: 1.2 3.5]). this relationship was dose dependent (adjusted odds ratio over 5 antibiotic courses: 3.0 [95% confidence interval: 1.6 5.6]), strongest for exposures within 1 year of diagnosis, and did not substantively change when adjusting for number or type of infections. in contrast, nonbacterial antimicrobial agents (eg, antifungal, antiviral) were not associated with jia. in addition, antibiotic-treated upper respiratory tract infections were more strongly associated with jia than untreated upper respiratory tract infections. conclusions: antibiotics were associated with newly diagnosed jia in a dose- and time-dependent fashion in a large pediatric population. antibiotic exposure may play a role in jia pathogenesis, perhaps mediated through alterations in the microbiome.

title: a novel approach to exploring the dark genome and its application to mapping of the vertebrate virus fossil record

abstract: abstract background genomic regions that remain poorly understood, often referred to as the dark genome, contain a variety of functionally relevant and biologically informative features. these include endogenous viral elements (eves) virus-derived sequences that can dramatically impact host biology and serve as a virus fossil record. in this study, we introduce a database-integrated genome screening (digs) approach to investigate the dark genome in silico, focusing on eves found within vertebrate genomes. results using digs on 874 vertebrate genomes, we uncover approximately 1.1 million eve sequences, with over 99% originating from endogenous retroviruses or transposable elements that contain eve dna. we show that the remaining 6038 sequences represent over a thousand distinct horizontal gene transfer events across 10 virus families, including some that have not previously been reported as eves. we explore the genomic and phylogenetic characteristics of non-retroviral eves and determine their rates of acquisition during vertebrate evolution. our study uncovers novel virus diversity, broadens knowledge of virus distribution among vertebrate hosts, and provides new insights into the ecology and evolution of vertebrate viruses. conclusions we comprehensively catalog and analyze eves within 874 vertebrate genomes, shedding light on the distribution, diversity, and long-term evolution of viruses and reveal their extensive impact on vertebrate genome evolution. our results demonstrate the power of linking a relational database management system to a similarity search-based screening pipeline for in silico exploration of the dark genome.

title: extraordinary increase in west nile virus cases and first confirmed human usutu virus infection in hungary, 2018
display_name: Extraordinary increase in West Nile virus cases and first confirmed human Usutu virus infection in Hungary, 2018
abstract: background during the 2018 wnv transmission season, similarly to other endemic areas in europe, a large number of human west nile virus (wnv) infections were reported in hungary. aims we summarise the epidemiological and laboratory findings of the 2018 transmission season and expand experiences in flavivirus differential diagnostics. methods every patient with clinical suspicion of acute wnv infection was in parallel tested for wnv, tick-borne encephalitis virus and usutu virus (usuv) by serological methods. sera, whole blood and urine samples were also tested for the presence of viral nucleic acid. results until the end of december 2018, 215 locally acquired and 10 imported human wnv infections were notified in hungary. all reported cases were symptomatic; most of them exhibited neurological symptoms. in a large proportion of tested individuals, whole blood was the most appropriate sample type for viral nucleic acid detection, but because whole blood samples were not always available, testing of urine samples also extended diagnostic possibilities. in addition, the first human usuv infection was confirmed in 2018 in a patient with aseptic meningitis. serological cross-reactions with wnv in different serological assays were experienced, but subsequent molecular biological testing and sequence analysis identified europe lineage 2 usuv infection. conclusion careful interpretation and simultaneous application of different laboratory methods are necessary to avoid misdiagnosis of human usuv cases. expansion of the laboratory-confirmed case definition criteria for detection of viral rna in any clinical specimens to include urine samples could increase diagnostic sensitivity.

title: recurrent kikuchi-fujimoto disease successfully treated by the concomitant use of hydroxychloroquine and corticosteroids
display_name: Recurrent Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease Successfully Treated by the Concomitant Use of Hydroxychloroquine and Corticosteroids
abstract: kikuchi-fujimoto disease (kfd) is a benign disease of unknown etiology characterized by lymphadenopathy and a fever. for the majority of patients with kfd, the course is self-limited; however, the optimum method of managing recurrent cases has not yet been established. we herein report a case of a 42-year-old japanese woman with kfd (confirmed by a lymph node biopsy). although high-dose prednisolone (psl) rapidly induced remission, she experienced four recurrences on treatment tapering. concomitant use of hydroxychloroquine (hcq) with low-dose psl induced continuous remission. this is the first case to suggest the effectiveness of hcq for recurrent kfd in a japanese patient.

title: chronic lyme disease and co-infections: differential diagnosis
display_name: Chronic Lyme Disease and Co-infections: Differential Diagnosis
abstract: in lyme disease concurrent infections frequently occur. the clinical and pathological impact of co-infections was first recognized in the 1990th, i.e. approximately ten years after the discovery of lyme disease. their pathological synergism can exacerbate lyme disease or induce similar disease manifestations. co-infecting agents can be transmitted together with borrelia burgdorferi by tick bite resulting in multiple infections but a fraction of co-infections occur independently of tick bite. clinically relevant co-infections are caused by bartonella species, yersinia enterocolitica , chlamydophila pneumoniae , chlamydia trachomatis , and mycoplasma pneumoniae . in contrast to the usa, human granulocytic anaplasmosis (hga) and babesiosis are not of major importance in europe. infections caused by these pathogens in patients not infected by borrelia burgdorferi can result in clinical symptoms similar to those occurring in lyme disease. this applies particularly to infections caused by bartonella henselae , yersinia enterocolitica , and mycoplasma pneumoniae . chlamydia trachomatis primarily causes polyarthritis. chlamydophila pneumoniae not only causes arthritis but also affects the nervous system and the heart, which renders the differential diagnosis difficult. the diagnosis is even more complex when co-infections occur in association with lyme disease. treatment recommendations are based on individual expert opinions. in antibiotic therapy, the use of third generation cephalosporins should only be considered in cases of lyme disease. the same applies to carbapenems, which however are used occasionally in infections caused by yersinia enterocolitica . for the remaining infections predominantly tetracyclines and macrolides are used. quinolones are for alternative treatment, particularly gemifloxacin. for bartonella henselae , chlamydia trachomatis , and chlamydophila pneumoniae the combination with rifampicin is recommended. erythromycin is the drug of choice for campylobacter jejuni .

title: role of erythropoietin receptor signaling in parvovirus b19 replication in human erythroid progenitor cells
display_name: Role of Erythropoietin Receptor Signaling in Parvovirus B19 Replication in Human Erythroid Progenitor Cells

authorships.name: Sai Lou
institutions: First Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University

authorships.name: Zhengwen Liu
institutions: First Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University

abstract: abstract parvovirus b19 (b19v) infection is highly restricted to human erythroid progenitor cells. although previous studies have led to the theory that the basis of this tropism is receptor expression, this has been questioned by more recent observation. in the study reported here, we have investigated the basis of this tropism, and a potential role of erythropoietin (epo) signaling, in erythroid progenitor cells (epcs) expanded ex vivo from cd34 + hematopoietic cells in the absence of epo (cd36 + /epo epcs). we show, first, that cd36 + /epo epcs do not support b19v replication, in spite of b19v entry, but epo exposure either prior to infection or after virus entry enabled active b19v replication. second, when janus kinase 2 (jak2) phosphorylation was inhibited using the inhibitor ag490, phosphorylation of the epo receptor (epor) was also inhibited, and b19v replication in ex vivo -expanded erythroid progenitor cells exposed to epo (cd36 + /epo + epcs) was abolished. third, expression of constitutively active epor in cd36 + /epo epcs led to efficient b19v replication. finally, b19v replication in cd36 + /epo + epcs required epo, and the replication response was dose dependent. our findings demonstrate that epor signaling is absolutely required for b19v replication in ex vivo -expanded erythroid progenitor cells after initial virus entry and at least partly accounts for the remarkable tropism of b19v infection for human erythroid progenitors.
classification_path: Natural Science > Biological Science > Microbiology > Virology

title: parvovirus b19 ns1 protein induces cell cycle arrest at g2-phase by activating the atr-cdc25c-cdk1 pathway
display_name: Parvovirus B19 NS1 protein induces cell cycle arrest at G2-phase by activating the ATR-CDC25C-CDK1 pathway
abstract: human parvovirus b19 (b19v) infection of primary human erythroid progenitor cells (epcs) arrests infected cells at both late s-phase and g2-phase, which contain 4n dna. b19v infection induces a dna damage response (ddr) that facilitates viral dna replication but is dispensable for cell cycle arrest at g2-phase; however, a putative c-terminal transactivation domain (tad2) within ns1 is responsible for g2-phase arrest. to fully understand the mechanism underlying b19v ns1-induced g2-phase arrest, we established two doxycycline-inducible b19v-permissive ut7/epo-s1 cell lines that express ns1 or ns1mtad2, and examined the function of the tad2 domain during g2-phase arrest. the results confirm that the ns1 tad2 domain plays a pivotal role in ns1-induced g2-phase arrest. mechanistically, ns1 transactivated cellular gene expression through the tad2 domain, which was itself responsible for atr (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated and rad3-related) activation. activated atr phosphorylated cdc25c at serine 216, which in turn inactivated the cyclin b/cdk1 complex without affecting nuclear import of the complex. importantly, we found that the atr-chk1-cdc25c-cdk1 pathway was activated during b19v infection of epcs, and that atr activation played an important role in b19v infection-induced g2-phase arrest.

title: seroepidemiology of chronic fatigue syndrome: a case-control study
display_name: Seroepidemiology of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Case-Control Study
abstract: abstract we performed serological testing for a large number of infectious agents in 26 patients from atlanta who had chronic fatigue syndrome (cfs) and in 50 controls matched by age, race, and sex. we did not find any agent associated with cfs. in addition, we did not find elevated levels of antibody to any of a wide range of agents examined. in particular, we did not find elevated titers of antibody to any herpesvirus, nor did we find evidence of enteroviral exposure in this group of patients.

title: metagenomic survey for viruses in western arctic caribou, alaska, through iterative assembly of taxonomic units
display_name: Metagenomic Survey for Viruses in Western Arctic Caribou, Alaska, through Iterative Assembly of Taxonomic Units

authorships.name: Jim Dau
institutions: Alaska Department of Fish and Game

authorships.name: Kimberlee B. Beckmen
institutions: Alaska Department of Fish and Game

authorships.name: Morten Tryland
institutions: UiT The Arctic University of Norway

abstract: pathogen surveillance in animals does not provide a sufficient level of vigilance because it is generally confined to surveillance of pathogens with known economic impact in domestic animals and practically nonexistent in wildlife species. as most (re-)emerging viral infections originate from animal sources, it is important to obtain insight into viral pathogens present in the wildlife reservoir from a public health perspective. when monitoring living, free-ranging wildlife for viruses, sample collection can be challenging and availability of nucleic acids isolated from samples is often limited. the development of viral metagenomics platforms allows a more comprehensive inventory of viruses present in wildlife. we report a metagenomic viral survey of the western arctic herd of barren ground caribou (rangifer tarandus granti) in alaska, usa. the presence of mammalian viruses in eye and nose swabs of 39 free-ranging caribou was investigated by random amplification combined with a metagenomic analysis approach that applied exhaustive iterative assembly of sequencing results to define taxonomic units of each metagenome. through homology search methods we identified the presence of several mammalian viruses, including different papillomaviruses, a novel parvovirus, polyomavirus, and a virus that potentially represents a member of a novel genus in the family coronaviridae.
